en.title: North Korea's post-pandemic transition: state re-centralization, military-industrial expansion and external reorientation
en.deck: North Korea has emerged from the border-closure shock with stronger state direction, recovering trade and industry, deeper Russia ties and a more institutionalized two-state posture, while household welfare, hidden military flows and the exact scale of nuclear capabilities remain difficult to measure.
en.regime: Post-pandemic managed re-centralization: official-sector recovery and external diversification coexist with persistent market dependence, sanctions, energy constraints and limited independent access.
en.key_risk: A growth model increasingly dependent on priority allocation and opaque Russia-linked earnings may strengthen strategic sectors without producing broad civilian productivity or household welfare gains; an external trade or security shock could expose that gap.

pt-BR.title: A transição pós-pandemia da Coreia do Norte: recentralização estatal, expansão militar-industrial e reorientação externa
pt-BR.deck: A Coreia do Norte saiu do choque do fechamento de fronteiras com maior direção estatal, recuperação do comércio e da indústria, vínculos mais profundos com a Rússia e postura de dois Estados mais institucionalizada, enquanto bem-estar doméstico, fluxos militares ocultos e a escala exata das capacidades nucleares continuam difíceis de medir.
pt-BR.regime: Recentralização administrada pós-pandemia: recuperação do setor oficial e diversificação externa coexistem com dependência persistente de mercados, sanções, restrições energéticas e acesso independente limitado.
pt-BR.key_risk: Um modelo de crescimento cada vez mais dependente de alocação prioritária e receitas opacas ligadas à Rússia pode fortalecer setores estratégicos sem gerar produtividade civil ampla ou ganhos de bem-estar doméstico; um choque comercial ou de segurança externo poderia expor essa lacuna.

key_constraints: No current independently administered nationwide household or enterprise survey accessible to outside researchers
Bank of Korea GDP and sector figures are model-based external estimates rather than DPRK national accounts
The UN Country Team has lacked normal in-country international access since early 2021 and the IAEA has had no inspectors in the DPRK since 2009
Energy availability, aging capital stock and sanctions constrain civilian industrial productivity
Recorded external trade remains highly concentrated in China while Russia-linked military and service flows are unusually opaque
Food access cannot be inferred directly from crop conditions because distribution, purchasing power and imports also matter
Defense-related output and foreign-exchange earnings are not transparently reported
selection_rationale: North Korea is undergoing a consequential post-pandemic structural transition: the state is reasserting control over strategic allocation, trade and distribution while preserving market mechanisms that became embedded after the 1990s; conventional trade with China has recovered; security and military-industrial relations with Russia have deepened; a new 2026–2030 development plan emphasizes state-led industrial and regional upgrading; and the inter-Korean framework is becoming more explicitly organized around two separate states. These changes connect economics, politics and society and materially affect Northeast Asian security and regional production relationships.
contrary_evidence: Three consecutive years of Bank of Korea-estimated real GDP growth above 3 percent, recovering merchandise trade and visible construction argue against a simple stagnation or collapse thesis, although the GDP figures remain external estimates.
Persistent household markets, foreign-currency use and informal procurement argue against describing current policy as a complete return to pre-1990s central planning.

China remains overwhelmingly dominant in observable conventional trade, limiting claims that North Korea has economically pivoted from China to Russia even as Russia has become more important strategically and militarily.

Generally favorable 2026 crop conditions observed by FAO do not establish nationwide food security because international field access and current representative household consumption data remain limited.

The continuation and apparent expansion of nuclear-related facilities are supported by remote observation, but the absence of IAEA inspectors since 2009 prevents direct verification of the exact stockpile or all facility activity.
limitations: Political and economic opacity requires combining sources with different incentives and methodologies; no single source class is treated as comprehensive.
DPRK official sources are used for declared policy, institutional texts and official claims rather than independent verification of outcomes.
ROK institutions are external estimators from a state in direct political and military competition with the DPRK; their methodologies are identified and cross-checked where possible.
Chinese customs measure declared merchandise trade but do not capture all unrecorded, sanctioned, military or service flows.

OHCHR findings rely substantially on interviews with people who left the DPRK and other external evidence because unrestricted contemporary in-country access is unavailable; representativeness limits are stated explicitly.
Russian official sources establish what Russia publicly acknowledges about cooperation and military participation, not independent estimates of battlefield effects or compensation.
